summary: Estonia is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities get 90 days in any 180-day period (ETIAS is not yet in operation), and everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa. Estonia restricts entry for Russian citizens holding a short-term Schengen visa.

RU.notes: A Schengen visa is required, and Estonia's government has restricted temporary entry, since 19 September 2022, for Russian citizens holding a short-term Schengen visa. Estonia also does not accept visa applications from Russian citizens except narrow groups, such as family members of Estonian citizens and residents, EU citizens' family members, people in international transport and humanitarian cases. The European Commission says that since 7 November 2025 Russian nationals no longer receive multiple-entry visas and must apply for a new visa for each trip, with exceptions for limited, justified cases such as independent journalists and human rights defenders.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travellers are registered in the EU Entry/Exit System when they enter the Schengen area for a short stay: on a first visit you may be asked to give fingerprints and a photo at a special booth before the immigration desk, and there is nothing to do before you reach the border. The UK government's travel advice says there is no cost for EES registration.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travellers will need an ETIAS travel authorisation to enter the Schengen Area. It is not yet in operation, and no applications are being collected; the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. The official EU site is travel-europe.europa.eu.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Arriving from outside the EU, the EU's Your Europe portal gives a duty-free allowance of 4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer, plus 1 litre of spirits (or 2 litres of fortified or sparkling wine), and other goods worth up to €300 (€430 by air or sea). It lists Estonia among the countries applying the lower tobacco limit to all travellers: 40 cigarettes, 20 cigarillos, 10 cigars or 50 g of tobacco. Travellers under 17 get no alcohol or tobacco allowance.
Between EU countries, alcohol and tobacco bought with tax paid, for your own use and not for resale, owe no further tax, according to the EU's Your Europe portal.

safety.text: The UK Foreign Office says pickpockets can be a problem in bars and nightclubs in Tallinn's Old Town, and that attacks, including sexual assaults, are rare but do occur, most often late at night around nightlife locations.

tips.text: Estonia's government has restricted temporary entry, since 19 September 2022, for Russian citizens holding a short-term Schengen visa, and Estonia no longer recognises non-biometric Russian passports.
Non-EU visitors are registered biometrically in the EU Entry/Exit System at the border, and the ETIAS travel authorisation for visa-exempt travellers is not yet in operation.
Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Finland are all in the Schengen Area, so days spent in any of them draw on the same 90-days-in-180 allowance rather than resetting it.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Estonia?
faq.answer: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely with a passport or ID card. Citizens of around 60 countries — including the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan — can visit visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period. Everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa (€90) from an Estonian mission or a Schengen state representing Estonia.

faq.question: Does time in Estonia count against my Schengen 90-day limit?
faq.answer: Yes. Estonia is fully in the Schengen Area, so days spent there count toward the single 90-days-in-180 allowance shared with all other Schengen countries.

faq.question: Can Russian citizens enter Estonia with a Schengen visa?
faq.answer: Only in narrow cases. Estonia's government has restricted temporary entry, since 19 September 2022, for Russian citizens holding a short-term Schengen visa, and Estonia accepts visa applications from Russian citizens only from narrow groups, such as family members of Estonian citizens and residents, EU citizens' family members, people in international transport and humanitarian cases. Questions about crossing the border go to the Estonian Police and Border Guard Board.

faq.question: Do I need ETIAS to visit Estonia?
faq.answer: Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, visa-exempt non-EU travellers will need the €20 online authorisation before travelling to Estonia and the rest of the Schengen Area. It is not yet in operation, and no applications are being collected; the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. The official EU site is travel-europe.europa.eu.

faq.question: Can I visit Helsinki from Tallinn without extra formalities?
faq.answer: Estonia and Finland are both in the Schengen Area, whose Borders Code abolishes routine checks at internal borders, and days in Finland draw on the same 90/180 allowance.
